title: Practice: Comparing Aerobic and Anaerobic Respiration

questions.stem: A sprinter runs a 100 m race in 10 seconds, while a marathon runner maintains a steady pace for over 2 hours. Which statement best explains the difference in their predominant respiration type?

options.text: The sprinter uses mainly aerobic respiration because it releases energy faster
The marathon runner relies mainly on anaerobic respiration for sustained energy
The sprinter relies heavily on anaerobic respiration because oxygen cannot be supplied fast enough
Both athletes use only aerobic respiration but at different rates

questions.explanation: During a short, intense sprint, the muscles demand energy so rapidly that the cardiovascular system cannot deliver oxygen fast enough. The sprinter therefore relies heavily on anaerobic respiration. The marathon runner maintains a pace where aerobic respiration can meet most energy needs.

questions.stem: A table compares two types of respiration. One column shows 'glucose → lactic acid' and the other shows 'glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water'. Which row correctly identifies further differences?

options.text: Lactic acid pathway: occurs in mitochondria, releases more energy
CO₂ + water pathway: occurs in the cytoplasm, releases less energy
Lactic acid pathway: occurs in the cytoplasm, releases less energy per glucose molecule
Both pathways occur in the mitochondria and release the same amount of energy

questions.explanation: Anaerobic respiration (glucose → lactic acid) occurs in the cytoplasm and releases far less energy per glucose molecule because glucose is only partially broken down. Aerobic respiration occurs in the mitochondria and releases much more energy.

questions.stem: A student argues that anaerobic respiration is 'better' because it does not require oxygen. What is the strongest scientific counter-argument?

options.text: Anaerobic respiration only occurs in plants, not animals
Anaerobic respiration produces toxic waste products and releases much less energy per glucose
Anaerobic respiration cannot use glucose as a fuel source
Anaerobic respiration takes longer than aerobic respiration

questions.explanation: While not needing oxygen is an advantage in low-oxygen conditions, anaerobic respiration is far less efficient — it releases much less energy per glucose molecule and produces lactic acid (in animals) which can be harmful at high concentrations.

questions.stem: Yeast cells are placed in two flasks: Flask A has plenty of oxygen, Flask B has no oxygen. Both contain glucose solution. After 24 hours, which observation would you expect?

options.text: Flask A produces ethanol; Flask B produces carbon dioxide and water
Flask A produces lactic acid; Flask B produces ethanol
Flask A produces carbon dioxide and water; Flask B produces ethanol and carbon dioxide
Both flasks produce identical products because yeast always ferments

questions.explanation: With oxygen (Flask A), yeast carries out aerobic respiration producing CO₂ and water. Without oxygen (Flask B), yeast switches to anaerobic respiration (fermentation), producing ethanol and CO₂. Yeast does not produce lactic acid — that is an animal cell product.

questions.stem: During a long swim, an athlete's muscles use both aerobic and anaerobic respiration simultaneously. Why might the body continue aerobic respiration even when anaerobic respiration is also occurring?

options.text: Aerobic respiration is needed to convert lactic acid into glucose
Aerobic respiration releases much more energy per glucose molecule, which is essential for sustained activity
Anaerobic respiration can only occur if aerobic respiration is also happening
The body cannot switch off aerobic respiration once it has started

questions.explanation: Aerobic respiration releases approximately 38 ATP per glucose compared to only 2 ATP from anaerobic respiration. The body maintains aerobic respiration as far as possible because it is far more efficient, only supplementing with anaerobic respiration when oxygen supply is insufficient.
